questions: Do I always play chords with my right hand?
Is Am/C the same as playing only C?

blocks.heading: Build C major
blocks.body: C–E–G is a C major triad. From C, E is four semitones higher and G is seven semitones higher. Find the three keys, play each once, then sound them together. Yamaha gives right-hand 1–3–5 as the usual root-position fingering for this example.
blocks.evidence_status: [已核实] factual core; [推断] editorial exercise/method where stated

blocks.heading: Change the middle note
blocks.body: Compare C–E–G with C–E♭–G. Lowering E by one semitone gives C minor. Compare the keyboard shapes and sound; the black key is E-flat in this chord’s spelling.
blocks.evidence_status: [已核实] factual core; [推断] editorial exercise/method where stated

blocks.heading: Practise a connection
blocks.body: Original exercise: play C4–E4–G4 for four counts, then C4–E4–A4 for four counts, and return. The second group is A minor in first inversion. C4 and E4 stay in place while G4 changes to A4. Plan the movement before counting in; use the chord chart to inspect each voicing. Fingering for this transition is not prescribed.
blocks.evidence_status: [已核实] factual core; [推断] editorial exercise/method where stated

/keyboard-notes/finger-numbers.title: Piano Finger Numbers: Left & Right Hand Chart
/keyboard-notes/finger-numbers.description: Learn piano finger numbers 1 to 5 for both hands. Read RH and LH examples and tell fingering apart from scale degrees and octave labels.
/keyboard-notes/finger-numbers.user_task: Identify the finger meant by a piano fingering number on either hand and follow the correct specific reference.
questions: Does LH 3 mean the third key from the left?
Does this chart tell me how to finger any song?

blocks.heading: Both thumbs are 1
blocks.body: Piano finger numbers use the same labels on both hands: thumb 1, index finger 2, middle finger 3, ring finger 4 and little finger 5. The little finger is also called the pinky. LH means left hand and RH means right hand. Start by checking the hand label as well as the number.

blocks.heading: Read each hand separately
blocks.body: The diagrams show the backs of your hands as you look down with your fingertips pointing away. The thumbs face inward. From left to right, the left-hand labels read 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, while the right-hand labels read 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. The fingers keep their identities when the picture is mirrored.

blocks.heading: A number identifies a finger
blocks.body: Finger 1 does not permanently mean C. A fingering mark says which finger is intended for that note in that passage. Published exercises can ask the same thumb to play C and then D. For a particular scale, chord or arpeggio, use its own stated hand, direction and range.

blocks.heading: Finger numbers and scale degrees
blocks.body: A finger number labels part of your hand. A scale degree labels a note’s position relative to the tonic. Finger 3 means the middle finger; scale degree 3 means the third degree of the scale. Reading one does not tell you the other.

blocks.heading: Try a quick identification check
blocks.body: Find the left thumb, then the right little finger. Name their numbers before checking the table. Next find finger 2 on each hand. This check only asks you to identify fingers; choose a specific scale or chord reference when you need instructions for playing notes.

blocks.heading: Read the table by scale degree
blocks.body: Each row stacks alternate notes from the selected scale. In major, the resulting qualities are major, minor, minor, major, major, minor and diminished. Uppercase Roman numerals indicate major triads; lowercase indicate minor, with ° for diminished.

blocks.heading: Keep minor forms explicit
blocks.body: The D minor table starts with natural minor: D E F G A B-flat C. It therefore includes A minor. The separate raised-leading-tone options use C-sharp, producing A major and C-sharp diminished; do not silently replace the natural-minor row.
blocks.evidence_status: [已核实] source formulas; [推断] original voicings/editorial examples

blocks.heading: Try a key-specific result
blocks.body: In E major, I–IV–V is E–A–B. Read the complete notes in each row before playing: E–G-sharp–B, A–C-sharp–E, then B–D-sharp–F-sharp. In F major, remember B-flat in the scale and its derived chords.

/chord-progressions.description: Compare I–V–vi–IV, I–vi–IV–V and I–IV–V–I in C, E and A major. Read exact four-bar examples and understand what the Roman numerals mean.

blocks.heading: Hear the sequence
blocks.body: A chord progression is an ordered sequence of harmonies. I–V–vi–IV becomes C–G–Am–F in C major, E–B–C-sharp minor–A in E major, and A–E–F-sharp minor–D in A major. The original examples below give a concrete register and four counts per chord.

blocks.heading: Compare three patterns
blocks.body: The collection includes I–V–vi–IV, I–vi–IV–V, and a four-bar I–IV–V–I practice example. Try the first two as loops, then compare the last pattern’s final return to I. The printable includes all three keys and every chord’s notes.
blocks.evidence_status: [已核实] source formulas; [推断] original voicings/editorial examples

blocks.heading: Explore an effect
blocks.body: For a “beautiful” starting point, try the I–vi–IV–V example slowly, sounding chord tones in sequence. For a “happy” starting point, try the I–IV–V–I example with light, even pulses. These are subjective playing suggestions: neither label is a property guaranteed by the chord order.

/chords/finder.title: Piano Chord Finder: Identify Chords from Notes
/chords/finder.description: Enter piano notes to inspect possible chord names. Keep bass notes and enharmonic spelling visible, and see when the supported vocabulary has no match.
/chords/finder.user_task: Identify candidate chords from notes rather than looking up a known name.
questions: Does an empty bass field mean the bass is unknown?
Does no match mean the notes are wrong?

blocks.heading: Enter what you actually play
blocks.body: Select the notes and, if known, the lowest sounding note. Repeated notes in different octaves do not add new pitch classes, but the bass and spacing still matter. E–G–C with E lowest can be C/E: a C major chord in first inversion.
blocks.evidence_status: [已核实] source formulas; [推断] original voicings/editorial examples

blocks.heading: Compare candidates
blocks.body: C, E, G and A can form C6 or Am7. The same keys alone do not establish one harmonic meaning. Read the bass and surrounding chords before choosing a label. The prepared examples display both interpretations where appropriate.
blocks.evidence_status: [已核实] source formulas; [推断] original voicings/editorial examples

blocks.heading: An incomplete answer can be useful
blocks.body: C and G contain no third, so this input does not decide between a C major and C minor triad. If a collection falls outside the supported vocabulary, keep the note list visible and show that no supported match has been confirmed.
blocks.evidence_status: [已核实] source formulas; [推断] original voicings/editorial examples
